clue.text: Line in fashionable clothing works for women

parts.note: chic means stylish or fashionable

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the word for clothes

parts.note: kit is an informal word for clothes or gear

explanation.surface: A fashion house sells a range of stylish garments suitable for the office, aimed at female customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' reads as a verb (clothing that works for women) but it is a noun: books. 'in' puts L inside KIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A genre label for light popular novels aimed at a female readership, so literary 'works' written for women.

clue.text: A very English mass with melodic piece — hymn in Latin

parts.note: M is the physics abbreviation for mass
an aria is a tuneful solo song in an opera

explanation.surface: A thoroughly Anglican church service includes a tuneful anthem sung in an ancient tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin prayer 'Hail Mary', widely sung in musical settings, is an example of a hymn in that language.

clue.text: Irksome boy's back in Hertfordshire town

indicators.note: in places that letter inside the name of the town

parts.note: Tring is a market town in Hertfordshire, a county just north of London

indicators.note: back points to the final letter of the word boy

explanation.surface: An annoying lad has returned to a town in the Home Counties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' picks the last letter of 'boy', Y, and 'in' puts it inside TRING, a small town in Hertfordshire, north of London. The surface suggests the boy has come back.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adjectives, synonyms for something annoying that tests your patience.

clue.text: Neglected group of colleges politician went round

parts.note: uni is short for university, which at Oxford or Cambridge is a group of colleges
an MP is a Member of Parliament
roved means wandered or went round from place to place

explanation.surface: A politician toured a cluster of run-down colleges that nobody had looked after.
explanation.definitionFit: Land or property left as it was, with no work done on it, is neglected; the two adjectives are near synonyms.

clue.text: Rejected portion of fresh soda bread

indicators.note: Rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
portion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A diner turns down a slice of newly baked Irish loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soda bread' is a loaf in the surface, but 'bread' alone is the definition, in its slang sense of money. 'portion of' finds HSOD in 'fresh soda' and 'Rejected' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang terms for money.

clue.text: Keep going round, covering central part of Russia and old area of France

indicators.note: covering says the first phrase wraps around the letters that follow

parts.note: a wheel that keeps going round will roll on

indicators.note: central part of takes the inner letters of Russia, leaving off its first and last

explanation.surface: A traveller's long circular tour takes in the Russian heartland and a historic French region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central part of' takes USSI from the middle of 'Russia', and 'covering' puts ROLL ON around it. The area is a former province in the far south of France, by the Pyrenees.
explanation.definitionFit: A historic province of southern France, abolished as an administrative unit at the Revolution, so a former region.

clue.text: Composer's limousine, short and lightweight

indicators.note: short says the word for the car loses its final letter

parts.note: a berlin is a type of limousine with a glass partition behind the driver
oz is the abbreviation for ounce, a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: A musician's chauffeured car is described as stubby and not very heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' removes the last letter of BERLIN, an old kind of limousine (originally a four-wheeled carriage), leaving BERLI. 'lightweight' is not an adjective here but a light weight: the ounce.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector, the French Romantic who wrote the Symphonie fantastique, is an example of a writer of music.

clue.text: Choke, suffocated by cut bread roll and tart

indicators.note: suffocated by says the first word is smothered inside the one that follows
cut says the word for the roll has its last letter removed

parts.note: a bagel is a ring-shaped bread roll
to gag is to choke or retch

explanation.surface: Someone at tea chokes, their airway blocked by a slice of bun and a pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all teatime, but 'tart' is no pastry: it is a dated, disparaging word for a brazen woman. 'cut' leaves BAGE for 'suffocated by' to wrap round the choking.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are old-fashioned insulting terms for a saucy or immoral woman.

clue.text: Bargain hunter maybe worried after he has opened faulty packs

indicators.note: after says the word for worried comes at the end, following the rest
has opened says the pronoun has got inside the rearranged letters
faulty says the letters of the next word are in the wrong order and must be put right

parts.note: something that ate at you worried you

explanation.surface: A shopper looking for deals is anxious once he has unwrapped some defective parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the shopper fretting; 'worried' really means gnawed at. 'faulty' makes CAPSK, which 'has opened' splits after its first letter, and 'after' sends the last piece to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingy person who hates paying full price might well go looking for discounts; 'maybe' marks it as one possible description.

clue.text: To begin with, sailors save returning boats

indicators.note: returning says the letters assembled so far are read from right to left
To begin with takes the opening letter of the word sailors

parts.note: save is a preposition meaning except, as is but

explanation.surface: The crew's first job is to rescue the vessels coming back to port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To begin with' gives S from 'sailors', which with BUT makes SBUT; 'returning' turns the whole lot round. 'save' is not rescue but the preposition meaning except.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang, slightly mocking term for slow or clumsy vessels.

clue.text: Traveller with problem: he runs about one kilometre

parts.note: a hitch is a snag or problem

indicators.note: about says the first two pieces go around the two that follow

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
K is an informal abbreviation for kilometre
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A tourist has a difficulty: he can only jog roughly a thousand metres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps HE and R around I and K, giving HIKER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gets around by begging lifts from passing drivers is one kind of person on a journey.

clue.text: Settled a debt unexpectedly, bringing in first of accountants

indicators.note: bringing in says the rearranged letters take another letter inside
unexpectedly says the letters before it turn up in a surprising new order
first of takes the opening letter of accountants

explanation.surface: Someone surprisingly pays off what they owe after hiring a bookkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settled' is not paid off but died down. 'unexpectedly' makes BTED, and 'bringing in' gives it the letter that 'first of' picks out.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm that has died down has subsided or become calm; the two verbs are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Record books preserved by community

indicators.note: preserved by says the books are kept safe inside the word that follows

parts.note: a nation is a large community of people
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A village keeps its old ledgers safe for posterity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'preserved by' puts OT, the Old Testament (a standard source of 'books'), inside NATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A written note or set of symbols is a way of setting something down; as a noun it is a near synonym.

clue.text: Held together pieces of eg thread

indicators.note: pieces of says the two words that follow are broken into their letters and reassembled

explanation.surface: Bits of something like cotton keep a garment from falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pieces of' breaks EG THREAD into its letters to be rearranged. In sewing, fabric drawn into folds by a thread is described by the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth pulled into small folds along a line of stitching is drawn up and kept in place, a sewing sense.

clue.text: Very blue foundation stones?

definitions.meaning: blue means pornographic, and the most explicit material of that kind is given this label
broken brick and rubble laid as the base layer of a road or building

explanation.definitionFit: It labels the most explicit pornography, and also names the rubble laid as a base under roads and buildings.

clue.text: Chapter in horror story mentioned furry rodent

indicators.note: mentioned says the word for the scary tale is spoken rather than written

parts.note: a chiller is a frightening story or film

explanation.surface: One section of a scary tale features a small fluffy animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mentioned' means CHILLER is said, sounding (in a British accent that drops the final R) like CHILLA.
explanation.definitionFit: A small South American gnawing mammal prized for its very soft grey coat, so an example of the animal described.

clue.text: Sombre Yank joins posh American, drinking spirit

indicators.note: joins says the word for pull is attached to the front of what follows

parts.note: to yank is to pull roughly, as is to lug

indicators.note: drinking says the two short pieces take the word for spirit inside them

parts.note: U is the old British label for upper-class speech and manners
US is the abbreviation for the United States, used as an adjective
brio is spirit or vivacity

explanation.surface: A gloomy man from the States meets a wealthy compatriot who is knocking back whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' wants to be an American; it is a verb, to pull, which 'joins' sets in front. 'posh' is the British class label U (upper-class usage), and 'drinking' is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adjectives meaning mournful or gloomy.

clue.text: Historian's account probing Roman emperor

indicators.note: probing says the abbreviation pushes its way into the name that follows

parts.note: Titus was emperor of Rome from AD 79 to 81

explanation.surface: A scholar's report looks closely into the life of a ruler of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote the Annals and the Histories of imperial Rome, so he is a well-known example of the profession.

clue.text: Line in trendy Beatles' song

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the word for trendy

parts.note: hep is dated slang for fashionable or in the know

explanation.surface: A lyric from a fashionable number by the Fab Four.
explanation.definitionFit: The title track of the band's 1965 film and album, so one example of their numbers.

clue.text: Steer and large bull

parts.note: to steer a vehicle is to drive it
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Two big farm animals, a bullock and a hefty male.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Steer' and 'bull' look like cattle. The first is a verb, to guide a vehicle; the second is slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for nonsense or rubbish talk.

clue.text: Choreographed work accompanying The Water Music?

definitions.text: Choreographed work accompanying The Water Music?

parts.words: Choreographed work accompanying The Water Music?
parts.note: the Handel suite is a decoy: read water music as music for the thing in a kitchen that water comes out of, and ask what set of steps would go with it

explanation.definitionFit: A stage routine performed in metal-tipped shoes, whose first word also names a source of running water, hence the joke.

clue.text: Declare Conservative will need a great deal … of this?

parts.note: to state is to declare
a raft of something is a large amount of it

explanation.surface: An announcement that a Tory politician is going to require plenty of some unnamed quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this' is the definition, and the whole clue gives it its meaning: a Conservative minister will need plenty of skill in running a country. 'will need' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of managing government affairs is what the clue as a whole says a politician requires plenty of.

clue.text: OK to run off with one and get married

parts.note: to leg it is British slang for to run away
the Roman numeral for one is I
to mate is to pair up or marry

explanation.surface: It's fine to elope with somebody and tie the knot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run off' is LEG IT, British slang for fleeing on foot; 'to', 'with' and 'and' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adjectives meaning lawful, valid or acceptable.

clue.text: Group of jobbing journalists swapping leaders in style of some writers

indicators.note: swapping leaders says the two words in the phrase exchange their opening letters

parts.note: hack is a word for a journalist who churns out work for hire, used here as a describing noun
a band is a group

explanation.surface: A team of freelance reporters trade bosses, as certain authors would describe it.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'group of jobbing journalists' is a HACK BAND; 'swapping leaders' exchanges the first letters of the two words. The 'writers' are people writing by hand, not authors.
explanation.definitionFit: Handwriting that slopes to the left is one manner in which people form their letters.

clue.text: African's talk about drugs given orally

parts.note: to gab is to chatter or talk
on means about, as in a book on birds

indicators.note: given orally says the plural of the drug is spoken rather than written

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so several are Es

explanation.surface: A discussion led by someone from Africa concerning medicines taken by mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'given orally' means Es (ecstasy tablets) is said, which sounds like the ending ESE. In the surface it describes medicine swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for something belonging to a person from a particular country on the west coast of central Africa.

clue.text: Position on scale controlled by man in charge

parts.note: someone who ran an organisation controlled it
a king is the man who rules a country

explanation.surface: A job grade determined by the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'controlled by' reads as a single phrase, but it splits: 'controlled' is a past-tense verb for managed, and 'by' only sets the monarch beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A place in an ordered list, such as a tennis player's world standing, is a place on a graded ladder.

clue.text: Being mean, strictly concealing every other component

indicators.note: concealing every other component says alternate letters of the two words before it are hidden away, leaving the rest

explanation.surface: Someone stingy keeps half the parts hidden, in true miserly fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' looks like a verb (being mean) but is a noun. 'concealing every other component' drops alternate letters of 'mean strictly', keeping the second, fourth and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are nouns for a thing that exists in its own right.

clue.text: Maybe rocker removing hat will reveal it?

indicators.note: removing hat says the word loses its top letter, the one worn on its head in a down entry

parts.note: a rocker, or rocking chair, is one kind of chair

explanation.surface: A rock musician who takes off his headgear might show what is underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing hat' takes the top letter, C, off CHAIR. 'it' is the definition, explained by the whole clue: what a rock fan shows on baring the head.
explanation.definitionFit: What grows on the head and comes into view when headgear is taken off, as the clue as a whole describes.
